issues: [security][critical][confidence:high] SIXTH recurrence of the same meta-defect, one layer below the one that was fixed. The name pool was abolished, but the rule that replaced it carries its own enumeration: `__has_shell_code_flag()` requires the code-delivery mechanism to be (a) a flag token matching ^-[A-Za-z]*c[A-Za-z]*$ and (b) followed by the code in argv. Both halves have real, present-on-this-machine counterexamples. Confirmed allow on HEAD **and** confirmed to actually delete the control plane in an isolated lab (cd into a fresh dir containing .claude/{settings.json,hooks}, run the exact string through a shell, verify .claude is gone): (1) `env -S "rm -rf .claude"` (2) `env -S 'rm -rf .claude'` (3) `/usr/bin/env -S "rm -rf .claude"` (4) `env -i -S "rm -rf .claude"` (5) `env -S "mv .claude /tmp/sink"` (6) `bash <<< 'rm -rf .claude'` (7) `sh <<< "rm -rf .claude"` (8) `zsh <<< 'rm -rf .claude'` (9) `dash <<< 'rm -rf .claude'` (10) `ksh <<< 'rm -rf .claude'` (11) `bash -s <<< "rm -rf .claude"` (12) `echo 'rm -rf .claude' | sh` (13) `printf '%s' 'rm -rf .claude' | bash`. Also `env -S 'rmdir .claude/hooks'` (allow; .claude/hooks actually removed). NOT a regression — parent deb3d08 and baseline 11c8db7 allow every one of these too; this sub-axis has never been closed. But it is the same axis the round claims to have converted from enumeration to structure, the deletion command sits in the payload as a plain quoted compound token exactly like `sh -c '…'`, and no other layer catches it.

[security][high][confidence:high] `env -S` is the direct counterexample to the flag-letter pool: it is a name-agnostic wrapper whose code flag is `-S`, not `-…c…`. Nothing about it is exotic — BSD `env -S` ships on this machine and splits its argument into an argv line. Any future or unknown tool whose code flag lacks a `c` is equally invisible. The rule went from 'which names are shells' (enumeration of ~5) to 'which letter means code' (enumeration of 1).

[security][high][confidence:high] Herestring / pipe / `-s` stdin delivery is the counterexample to the argv assumption: `bash <<< '…'`, `sh -s <<< '…'`, `echo '…' | sh` deliver the identical shell text with no code flag at all. `__find_wrapped_arg()` can only ever look at tokens that follow a flag, so this family is structurally invisible to both passes.

[security][high][confidence:high] Neither family is declared anywhere in `_residual_risk_AC11.open_axes_2026_08_04` (grep for `stdin`, `<<<`, `env -S`, `파이프` in sprint-51.json returns nothing relevant). SC-9's second clause requires unclosed axes to be listed there and not claimed closed. They are unclosed, unlisted, and covered by a closure-scope claim (next issue).

[docs][high][confidence:high] sprint-51.json line 112 `_note` and line 204/205 `interpreter_wrapped_path_notation` assert more than the evidence supports: '래퍼 이름 축은 이번에 열거 자체를 없애 이 함정에서 **원리적으로** 벗어났다 — 앞으로 이 축에 대해서는 … "이름을 보지 않는 구조 규칙이 실제로 이름과 무관하게 동작하는가"**만** 검증하면 된다' and '이번에는 옆 풀을 넓히는 대신 **없앴다**'. The first sentence prescribes a future verification scope that would never have found any of the 13 payloads above; the second is false as stated — one pool was removed and two others (flag letter, delivery mechanism) now bound coverage in its place. This is precisely the 'declare the axis escaped, get falsified next round' pattern the note itself is trying to break, and it is the sixth instance. The narrower, factual claims in the same file ('이 축은 이름을 전혀 보지 않는다', '구조 규칙') ARE accurate and verified — the defect is the scope words layered on top of them.

[test][high][confidence:high] The new decision↔execution equivalence test (tests/pre-bash-firewall.bats:3191) repeats the 23rd verdict's tautology one layer down. Its flag pool is `-c` plus filler letters (`cluster_flags`, `flag_notations`) — i.e. the test's flag pool mirrors `__has_shell_code_flag()`'s own regex, exactly as the old `wrappers` pool mirrored `WRAP_SHELL_TOKENS`. There is no cell in which the code flag is a different letter (`env -S`) or absent (`<<<`, pipe), so the test cannot in principle observe the 13 payloads above. Passing it is therefore not evidence about the axis, only about the sub-space the implementation already handles.

[test][medium][confidence:high] The strongest structural property of this round ('the rule never reads the name') is pinned by exactly one hard-coded cell (`notarealshell987`). SC-9's positive criterion asks for pools, not instances: the fictional-name axis should be generated (several unrelated fictional names × the same notation pool), the way the shell pool now is. My own sweep needed 4 fictional names + 4 prefix forms to be convincing; the suite has 1.

[quality][medium][confidence:high] Pass 1 accumulates candidates quadratically with no cap: for every token matching the flag shape it appends every remaining token, so a segment of k such tokens produces ~k²/2 candidates, and the array is fully built BEFORE the 3000 ms candidate budget is ever consulted. Measured worst case within the 2048-char segment cap and the 32768-byte entry cap: HEAD 4.27 s vs parent 1.65-1.78 s on the same input (12-14 quote-heavy 2040-char segments followed by one 680×`-c` segment), i.e. 2.4-2.6× the parent and only ~0.7 s under the hook's 5 s timeout on an otherwise idle machine. The 18th verdict already established that this machine's timing swings by an order of magnitude under load. The decision itself stays fail-closed (ask), and a hook timeout falls through to the native prompt rather than an allow, so this is a robustness/latency concern, not a fail-open — but it consumes most of the headroom the 17th/18th verdicts deliberately built.

[quality][low][confidence:medium] The `-e`/`-r` name gate is defensible on friction grounds (my 97-command corpus confirms `grep -e`, `perl -pe`, `perl -ne` stay allow, and generalising `-e` structurally would plausibly break them), but it leaves the pool split in two with different rules. Concrete consequence: `osascript -e 'do shell script "rm -rf .claude"'` is allow on HEAD and actually deletes .claude (verified in lab); osascript is not in INTERPRETER_ARM. This particular instance would also survive a name-gate fix because the shell text sits inside an AppleScript string literal, so I classify it under the already-declared `interpreter_shell_reentry` axis rather than as a new SC-9 violation — but it shows the `-e` gate's name pool has the same unbounded-membership problem the `-c` path just escaped.

[test][low][confidence:high] Still open from the 19th-23rd verdicts: no test pins the byte-vs-character measurement with actual 4-byte characters. tests/pre-bash-firewall.bats:3053+ builds its oversize payloads from ASCII 'x' only, so reverting `wc -c` to `${#CMD}` — the exact defect the 18th verdict rejected — would not fail any test.

[test][low][confidence:high] Still open: no test at the exact 32768-byte boundary. The suite exercises 30000 and 40000 bytes; the `-gt 32768` comparison itself (off-by-one in either direction) is untested.

[quality][low][confidence:high] Still open: `CMD_BYTES=$(printf '%s' "$CMD" | wc -c …)` keeps BSD wc's leading whitespace (verified: `printf 'abc' | wc -c` → "       3\n"). Harmless today because both uses are `[[ -z ]]` and `[[ … -gt … ]]` (arithmetic context tolerates it), but it is a latent trap for any future string comparison or export. A `tr -d ' '` or `$(( ))` normalisation would close it.

[observation][low][confidence:high] Not introduced by this round, but worth recording: `scan_control_plane_delete()` is gated behind `PURE_READ -eq 0`, so the whole unwrap path is skipped for read-classified tools. This is why `grep -c "rm -rf .claude" audit.log` and `wc -c "rm -rf .claude"` stay allow while `tar -czf backup.tgz "rm -rf .claude"` and `comm -c "mv .claude /tmp"` newly ask. It cuts both ways — it is also the reason the `-c` generalisation produced no measurable friction.

missing_criteria: No axis anywhere in sprint-51.json for **code-delivery mechanism** (argv-after-flag vs stdin/herestring/pipe vs env -S style argv splitting). Every wrapper axis so far has silently assumed argv-after-flag. This is the pool that broke this round and it has no name yet.

ambiguous_criteria: AC-11 verification_axes_2026_09_06 axis 1 now defines 'wrapper' BY the implementation's rule ('-…c… 모양 플래그를 가진 토큰'). Defining the axis as whatever the code does makes it unfalsifiable — the axis and the implementation can never disagree. The axis should be defined by the threat ('a command that receives shell text and executes it'), with the flag shape as one covered mechanism among several.
criteria_gaps.action_required: Before the next round, sprint-51.json must (a) add `wrapper_code_delivery_mechanism` to open_axes with the env -S and stdin families named and marked unresolved, (b) delete or rewrite the '원리적으로 벗어났다 / …만 검증하면 된다 / 없앴다' sentences at lines 112, 204, 205 so no closure scope is claimed beyond 'the name sub-axis is name-blind, independently verified', and (c) restate the wrapper axis in threat terms rather than in terms of the implementation's regex.

recommended_fix.primary: Do NOT add `-S` to the flag pool, and do NOT add `<<<` to a list of redirections — that is the fifth-and-sixth-time move this round was supposed to stop making. The generalisation that matches the two fixes that actually held (22nd: stop asking which options take values, try every candidate; 23rd: stop asking which names are shells, look at the flag shape) is: **stop asking how the code reaches the interpreter.** Concretely: if a segment contains any compound token (a quoted token containing whitespace) at all, unwrap it and re-scan it, regardless of what precedes it, what flag precedes it, or whether any flag precedes it. That subsumes -c, -S, herestrings, `echo … | sh`, and every future mechanism in one rule, and it needs no pool. The add-only property is unchanged: a compound token that does not unwrap to a delete verb + control-plane path costs nothing. My 97-command everyday corpus contains 21 commands with quoted compound tokens and none of them would flip (their contents are not delete-verb + control-plane-path), so the friction cost of this generalisation is measurable in advance rather than assumed.
secondary: If the above is judged too broad, the narrower honest alternative is to leave the code as is and make the DOCUMENT correct: declare `wrapper_code_delivery_mechanism` as an open axis with the 13 payloads listed, drop the 'principally escaped' language, and accept that SC-9 remains unmet for this axis. That would not raise the security score, but it would end the six-round pattern of a falsifiable closure claim.

Cap the pass-1 candidate accumulation (e.g. stop appending once the array exceeds a few thousand entries and set the fail-closed ask reason that already exists) so the array construction cannot outrun the budget check that is supposed to bound it.

Make the equivalence test's flag axis generative over the *mechanism*, not the letter: at minimum one cell whose flag letter is not `c` and one cell with no flag at all, so the test can fail when the rule's boundary is wrong.
Close the three long-open low items in the same pass: a 4-byte-character oversize test, an exact-32768-byte boundary test, and whitespace normalisation on CMD_BYTES.
recommended_fix.note: This verdict deliberately does not hand the implementer a list to close one by one. The 13 payloads are evidence that the boundary is in the wrong place, not a work list — closing exactly those 13 and declaring the axis handled would be the seventh instance of the pattern.
